summary:
We developed SpacePatch, a physiological monitoring prototype conceived as a lightweight patch for tracking astronauts’ cardiovascular activity. Its architecture integrates electrocardiographic signal acquisition, signal conditioning and quality assessment, wireless communication, and a real-time visualization platform. The proposed system incorporates artificial intelligence analysis to identify relevant changes and generate advisory alerts that support timely review.

SpacePatch addresses the space health monitoring challenge by connecting physiological data collection with interpretation and visualization in a decision-support tool. Its specialized approach aims to facilitate continuous cardiac monitoring and communicate potential risk situations without requiring constant manual inspection of recordings.

Its importance lies in providing information that can support decisions concerning crew well-being and operational continuity. Integration into a patch format aims to reduce equipment bulk and facilitate everyday use. The system remains experimental and requires clinical validation and evaluation under spaceflight conditions before supporting medical decisions.
details:
SpacePatch is a prototype for monitoring astronauts’ cardiovascular activity, conceived as a lightweight patch. It uses electrodes and an AD8232 sensor to acquire electrocardiographic signals at 500 samples per second. An ESP32 transmits the data over Wi-Fi to a computer for real-time visualization and CSV export.

The software integrates an experimental logistic regression model trained on WESAD. It analyzes heart rate and variability between beats to explore patterns associated with stress. Before interpreting a window, it checks electrode disconnections, missing samples, and signal quality.

We developed the firmware in C++ using Visual Studio Code and PlatformIO, the processing software in Python with NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn, and the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. An external battery powers the hardware.

Its creative contribution combines acquisition, communication, analysis, and visualization within a specialized patch concept. The intended benefit is accessible physiological monitoring that supports timely review during demanding operations.

Our team considered comfort, energy consumption, privacy, transmission stability, false positives, and differences between individuals. The prototype requires further validation. To demonstrate alerts, it includes an explicitly simulated scenario that appears after ten seconds while preserving the received ECG.
